**Drink type matters mostly through alcohol content and how fast it's absorbed.** Beer, wine, and spirits don't intoxicate you differently in themselves. One standard drink of any of them contains the same alcohol. What differs:
- **How much alcohol is actually in your glass.** A strong IPA or heavy pour can be close to two drinks.
- **Absorption speed.** Carbonation, diet mixers, and mid-strength cocktails get into your blood faster than still, sweet, or dilute drinks.
- **How fast you tend to drink it.** Shots go down in seconds, while a beer usually gets sipped.

The idea that "tequila makes me crazy" or "wine makes me sleepy" mostly comes from those differences plus the setting you drink in, not from the type of alcohol. Darker liquors do contain more byproducts called congeners, but those mainly affect how bad your hangover is, not how drunk you get.

**Bottom line:** the total amount limits how drunk you could get, but speed, food, and drink choice decide how close you come to that limit and how sharply you get there.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text: I want to know how to manage how drunk I feel, based on the speed or the amount that I drink.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
Good question — and understanding this well is one of the best ways to drink in a way that stays enjoyable. Here's how it actually works and how to use it.

## The core principle: your liver is a fixed-rate machine

Your body clears alcohol at a roughly constant rate — about **one standard drink per hour** (it varies a bit by person, but not by much, and you can't speed it up with coffee, water, food, or exercise).

So your blood alcohol level at any moment is basically:

**(what you've put in) − (what your liver has removed so far)**

This means **pace matters more than total**. Four drinks over four hours leaves you mildly buzzed; four drinks in one hour leaves you quite drunk, even though the total is identical.

## What counts as "one drink"

- 12 oz (355 ml) of ~5% beer
- 5 oz (150 ml) of ~12% wine
- 1.5 oz (45 ml) of 40% spirits

Watch for the traps: a pint of 7% IPA is ~1.7 drinks, a generous restaurant pour of wine is ~1.5, and a cocktail can easily be 2–3. Many people who feel "surprisingly" drunk simply miscounted.

## Managing how you feel

**To stay at a light buzz:**
Roughly one drink per hour. You'll plateau at a low level rather than climbing.

**To avoid overshooting:**
Alcohol takes **30–90 minutes to fully hit your bloodstream**. If you drink quickly, you'll feel okay at the moment you finish your third drink — but you still have two drinks' worth "in the pipeline" that haven't arrived yet. This lag is the main reason people end up drunker than intended. Rule of thumb: however you feel right now, you'll feel noticeably more intoxicated in 30 minutes if you've been drinking in the last hour.

**Food:** Eating before or while drinking slows absorption significantly — it doesn't lower your eventual peak much if you drink a lot, but it flattens and delays the curve, making it easier to pace.

**Water between drinks:** Doesn't sober you up, but it slows your drinking pace, reduces dehydration (a big part of hangovers), and fills you up.

**Body weight and sex:** Smaller people and (on average) women reach a higher blood alcohol level from the same amount, because there's less water in the body to dilute it. Adjust your "one per hour" accordingly — for some people it's closer to 0.7 per hour.

## Reading your own signals

| Approximate feeling | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Relaxed, warm, talkative | Light — easy to maintain with slow pacing |
| Noticeably looser, slightly less coordinated | Moderate — stop or slow for an hour to hold here |
| Slurring, balance off, decisions feel easy | You're past the point where you can judge well; stop now, more is already on the way |

## Practical tactics

- **Set a number before you start** and count honestly, including strong beers and generous pours.
- **Alternate** alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks.
- **Don't "catch up"** if you arrive late — that's the single most common way to overshoot.
- **Avoid shots** if your goal is control; they deliver a full drink in seconds with no natural pacing.
- **Slow down earlier than feels necessary** — remember the lag.
- **Sobering up is slow and non-negotiable**: if you've had 5 drinks, you're roughly 4–5 hours from being near zero. Plan transportation accordingly, and never estimate your own fitness to drive — you're unreliable at exactly the time it matters.

The short version: **spread drinks out to about one an hour, eat something, count accurately, and remember you're always 30 minutes behind your real level.**

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: If I had like 4 beers in two hours would that get me drunk?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Short answer: **yes, probably — moderately.** Not sloppy-drunk for most people, but clearly buzzed and likely over the legal driving limit.

## The math

- 4 beers in → 2 hours of liver work removes ~2 → roughly **2 drinks' worth** still in your system at the end
- But it's not a straight 2-drink feeling, because BAC depends on body size. Rough estimates for 4 standard (5%) beers over 2 hours:

| Person | Approx. peak BAC | How it feels |
|---|---|---|
| ~200 lb man | ~0.06 | Relaxed, talkative, warm — definite buzz |
| ~160 lb man | ~0.08 | Loosened up, coordination slipping a bit, judgment softer |
| ~140 lb woman | ~0.11–0.13 | Clearly drunk — balance off, possibly slurring |
| ~120 lb woman | ~0.14+ | Quite drunk |

(For reference, 0.08 is the US driving limit; 0.05 in many other countries.)

## Things that shift it

- **Beer strength is the big one.** Four 7% IPAs in pint glasses is really ~7 standard drinks, which pushes everyone in that table up a full tier or more.
- **Empty stomach** → faster, higher peak. Full meal → smoother and lower.
- **Timing within the two hours.** Four beers evenly spaced feels different from three in the first 40 minutes.
- **Tolerance** changes how drunk you *feel*, not your actual BAC or your reaction time.

## What to expect afterward

If you stop at 4, you'll likely feel your peak **about 30–45 minutes after the last beer**, not at the moment you finish it. From there it's roughly **4–5 more hours** before you're near zero — so don't plan on driving that night. Two hours after your last beer you might feel "fine," but you'd still be around 0.05–0.08 for an average-sized person.

If your goal is a buzz without crossing into drunk, **4 beers over 3–4 hours** instead of 2 would get you there and hold you there.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: Does doing coke actually make you feel less drunk, or how does that work?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Yes, it does — but it's worth understanding *why*, because the mechanism is exactly what makes the combination more dangerous than either alone.

## What's actually happening

**Alcohol is a depressant.** It slows your central nervous system — that's the fuzziness, slowed reactions, sleepiness, loosened coordination.

**Cocaine is a stimulant.** It floods your brain with dopamine and norepinephrine — alertness, energy, confidence, focus.

When you combine them, the stimulant **masks the sedating effects** of the alcohol. You feel sharper, more awake, more coordinated, more "with it." But your blood alcohol level hasn't changed at all. Your liver is still clearing one drink an hour. You're exactly as drunk as you were — you just can't feel it.

So the honest answer is: **you don't get less drunk, you lose your ability to perceive how drunk you are.** Which is a very different thing.

## Why that matters practically

Remember from earlier — your sense of how drunk you feel is your main tool for pacing. Cocaine removes that tool. The predictable result:

- **You drink much more than you otherwise would.** The "I've had enough" signal never arrives. People who'd normally stop at 5 drinks end up at 10–12 without noticing.
- **The alcohol is still fully there.** When the cocaine wears off (which happens fast — 20–60 minutes per line), you're suddenly hit with everything you drank, all at once. People go from "feeling great" to vomiting, blacking out, or passing out quickly, and this is where alcohol poisoning cases come from.
- **Judgment is impaired but confidence is high.** This is the worst combination for decisions about driving, fights, or anything risky — you feel capable and you aren't.

## The part most people don't know: cocaethylene

When alcohol and cocaine are in your body at the same time, your liver produces a third compound called **cocaethylene**. It isn't in either drug — your body manufactures it from the two.

- It's **more toxic to the heart** than cocaine alone, and raises the risk of heart attack, dangerous arrhythmias, and stroke — including in young, healthy people
- It **lasts 3–5 times longer** than cocaine, so the cardiac strain continues well after the high fades
- It's **harder on the liver**
- It also **extends and intensifies the euphoria**, which is part of why the combination is so compelling and why people redose more

The risk of sudden death from cocaine is estimated to be substantially higher when alcohol is involved — this combination is responsible for a disproportionate share of cocaine-related deaths and ER visits.

## If someone is going to do it anyway

Harm reduction basics, since the reality is this combination is common:

- **Count drinks by number, not by feel** — your feel is broken. Set a hard cap before the night starts.
- **Expect the crash.** When the stimulant wears off, the alcohol lands hard. Don't be somewhere unsafe when that happens.
- **Absolutely no driving.** You'll feel fine. You're not.
- **Watch for chest pain, racing/irregular heartbeat, severe headache, or confusion** — these are emergencies, not "ride it out" symptoms. Call for help and tell responders exactly what was taken; they're there to treat, not arrest.
- **Fentanyl contamination** in cocaine is a real and rising problem. Mixing an opioid with alcohol is a direct respiratory-depression risk. Test strips exist; naloxone is worth having around.

The bottom line: cocaine doesn't sober you up, it hides your drunkenness from you while adding a separate cardiac risk on top. It's one of the more dangerous common combinations precisely *because* it feels so good and so manageable in the moment.

transcript.label: P1
transcript.text: My buddy swears by it at parties so he can drink all night without crashing.

transcript.label: P1
transcript.text:
Your buddy isn't wrong about what he *experiences* — that's the thing. From the inside, it genuinely works. He feels sharp, he keeps going, he doesn't hit the wall at 1am. The problem is that what he's describing as "not crashing" is actually "not noticing."

## What's really happening to him over a night

Say he drinks from 9pm to 3am. That's six hours — his liver clears about 6 drinks in that window. If he's drinking at a party pace all night with the stimulant masking the sedation, he's probably putting away 12–15. So at 3am he's walking around with the equivalent of 6–9 drinks in his system, feeling like he's had 3.

That's not "drinking all night without crashing." That's **being very drunk while unable to tell.** The alcohol is all still there — it's just been hidden from him.

## "He's been fine every time" doesn't mean what it seems to

A few things worth knowing about why his track record isn't the reassurance it feels like:

- **Cocaethylene risk is cumulative and random.** The cardiac events it causes — arrhythmias, heart attacks in people in their 20s and 30s — don't ramp up with warning signs. They happen on an ordinary night that felt like every other night. Most people who have one had done it dozens of times before without a problem.
- **He's also been lucky on the alcohol side.** Someone at 0.20+ BAC who feels sober is one bad decision from a car, a fight, a fall, or passing out in the wrong place.
- **The fentanyl issue is a dice roll he's taking every time** on a supply he can't see into. Coke contaminated with fentanyl plus a heavy alcohol load is a respiratory-arrest combination, and it doesn't care about tolerance or experience.
- **He also can't be a reliable judge of his own state** — that's the whole mechanism. Everyone on coke and alcohol thinks they're handling it well. That's the drug talking.

## The crash he thinks he's skipping

He's not avoiding it, he's relocating it. Instead of getting tired at 1am and going home, he gets the whole thing at once when the stimulant runs out — usually a brutal comedown, often with a hangover that's noticeably worse than alcohol alone, plus the cardiac strain lingering for hours after. People who do this regularly tend to describe their next day as a different category of rough.

## What you can actually say to him

You probably can't talk him out of it, and lecturing won't help. But a few things are worth putting in his head:

- **"You're not less drunk, you just can't feel it."** That one line is the whole thing. If it lands, he might start counting drinks instead of going by feel.
- **Test strips for the coke.** Cheap, fast, and the fentanyl risk is the one most likely to kill someone young.
- **Hard drink cap, decided sober.** Not "when I feel it" — a number.
- **Never driving, no matter how fine he feels.** He'll feel very fine. That's the trap.
- **Know the emergency signs** — chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, confusion. Those are 911, not "drink some water." And tell responders exactly what was taken.

And honestly — the fact that he *needs* something to drink all night is worth noticing. The tiredness is his body's pacing signal. Overriding it chemically every weekend isn't a hack, it's removing the brakes.

transcript.label: P2
transcript.text: If people are gonna end up trying a bump while drinking anyway, isn't it way riskier not knowing the exact amounts or timing?

transcript.label: P2
transcript.text:
You're making a real argument — that's the whole logic of harm reduction, and it's usually right. People who know what they're taking, how much, and when are safer than people who don't. For most drugs, I'd agree without hesitation.

But this particular combination is one where "know the exact amounts and timing" breaks down, and it's worth being straight about why rather than pretending there's a safe recipe.

## Why precise dosing doesn't fix this one

**You can't know the amount.** Street cocaine ranges from roughly 20% to 90% pure, and the same bag varies from one end to the other. A "bump" could be 10mg of cocaine or 40mg. There's no way to dose precisely something you can't measure, and no way to measure something whose contents you don't know. That's not a knowledge gap you can close with better information — it's structural.

**The cardiac risk isn't a dose threshold.** With alcohol, risk scales fairly predictably with amount. With cocaethylene, the dangerous events — arrhythmias, coronary spasm, sudden cardiac death — are closer to a lottery than a dial. Small amounts have killed healthy young people; large amounts have been survived repeatedly. Knowing you took "a small amount" tells you less than you'd want it to.

**The thing you'd be timing is the thing the drug breaks.** Normally the whole point of pacing is to use your perception of your state as feedback. Cocaine removes that feedback loop. So "I'll just time it carefully" is a plan that depends on a faculty the plan itself disables.

**Fentanyl doesn't care about your dosing.** Any amount of contaminated product plus a few drinks is a respiratory risk. That's not something you manage through timing.

So the honest answer is: there is no amount or schedule I could give you that would make cocaine plus alcohol safe, and anyone who gives you one is making it up. That's not me dodging — it's the actual pharmacology.

## What does actually reduce risk

The things that help are mostly not about amounts and timing — they're about removing variables and keeping someone watching.

- **Test it.** Fentanyl test strips are cheap, take two minutes, and address the single most likely way a young person dies from this. Reagent kits can also flag levamisole and other common cuts. This is the highest-value thing on the list by a wide margin.
- **Have naloxone around.** If the strips were skipped or wrong, this is the backstop. It does nothing for cocaine or alcohol, but it's the difference between alive and not if there's an opioid in the mix.
- **Less is genuinely less.** A single small bump once in a night is a different risk profile from redosing every 30 minutes for six hours. The cocaethylene exposure, the heart strain, and the alcohol overshoot all scale with how long you keep the stimulant going. If someone's going to try it, trying it is less dangerous than *using it as a tool* the way your buddy does.
- **Don't redose to chase the drop.** The crash after each line is the main reason people keep going. Decide beforehand: one, and done.
- **Set the drink cap before the bump, not after.** Your "I've had enough" signal is about to go offline. Write the number down if you have to.
- **Nothing else in the mix.** No other stimulants, no benzos, no other downers. Each addition multiplies unpredictability.
- **Someone sober-ish knows what was taken.** Not to babysit — so that if something goes wrong, the person calling for help can say exactly what it was. That changes what paramedics do and how fast.
- **Know the stop signs and act on them.** Chest pain or pressure, heartbeat that's pounding, racing, or skipping, severe sudden headache, confusion, very high body temp, or someone who can't be woken. These are "call now," not "walk it off." You won't get arrested for calling about a friend.
- **No driving. No swimming. No heights.** Confidence will be very high and coordination will be very low, and the person won't be able to tell.

## The real answer to your question

You're right that ignorance is dangerous. But the most important thing to know about this combination isn't a number — it's that **the feeling of control it gives you is the drug, not reality.** Someone who understands that and still tries a bump once is in a much better position than someone who thinks they've found a technique. Your buddy's problem isn't that he lacks dosing information. It's that he's built a routine around a feedback signal he's chemically disabled, and he's been lucky enough that nothing has corrected him yet.

transcript.text: I want to know how to manage how drunk I feel, based on the speed or the amount that I drink.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
Here's how it actually works, and how to use it.

## The core principle: your liver is a fixed-rate machine

Your liver clears alcohol at roughly **one standard drink per hour** (about 0.015% BAC/hour), and you can't speed that up. Coffee, cold showers, food, water — none of these make you sober faster. What they *can* do is affect how fast alcohol enters your blood in the first place.

So the equation is simple: **how drunk you feel = (rate alcohol goes in) − (fixed rate it comes out)**.

A "standard drink" = 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 40% spirits. A lot of what people pour is 1.5–2 standard drinks, which is why counting "drinks" often misleads.

## Managing speed (the bigger lever)

- **One standard drink per hour** keeps most people hovering at a mild buzz rather than climbing. Two per hour will steadily push you up.
- **Front-loading is the trap.** Three drinks in the first 45 minutes puts you on a trajectory you can't undo — your BAC keeps rising for 30–90 minutes *after* your last sip as your stomach finishes absorbing. If you feel "fine" after chugging, you're not done yet.
- **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** This doesn't dilute alcohol in your body meaningfully, but it slows your pace, keeps your hands busy, and reduces dehydration (which worsens the hangover, not the drunkenness).
- **Eat before and during.** Food — especially fat and protein — slows stomach emptying, so alcohol hits your bloodstream more gradually. Drinking on an empty stomach can spike you noticeably harder from the same amount.
- **Lower-ABV, bigger-volume drinks** (beer, spritzers, long cocktails) are naturally slower than shots or neat spirits. Carbonation speeds absorption slightly, but the volume effect usually dominates.

## Managing amount

Rough BAC guide for someone around 160 lb who drinks over ~2 hours with food:
- **1–2 drinks**: light buzz, relaxed, ~0.02–0.04%
- **3–4 drinks**: clearly tipsy, judgment softening, ~0.06–0.08% (legal limit territory)
- **5–6 drinks**: drunk, coordination off, ~0.10–0.14%
- **7+**: heading toward sick/blackout risk

Adjust for yourself: smaller body or less muscle = higher BAC per drink; women typically reach higher BAC than men of the same weight on the same intake; being tired, sick, or on certain medications amplifies effects.

## Practical rules of thumb

1. **Decide your number before you start**, and count actual standard drinks, not glasses.
2. **Pace to the clock**, not to the group. Finish a drink, then wait before the next.
3. **Eat something real** in the hour before.
4. **If you're climbing faster than you want, stop early** — remember the 30–90 minute lag. Don't wait until you feel too drunk to stop; by then you'll get drunker anyway.
5. **Give yourself ~1 hour per drink** before you're truly back to baseline, and more before driving. Feeling "fine" is not the same as being sober.

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: Just in general. What sort of choices make the alcohol hit you faster or slower?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Here's the full list, grouped by what you can actually control.

## The drink itself

**Hits faster:**
- **Higher ABV in smaller volume** — shots, neat spirits, strong cocktails. Concentrated alcohol (roughly 20–30% range) absorbs fastest. Interestingly, very high concentrations (straight 40%+ spirits) can slightly irritate the stomach and slow emptying, but the dose is so concentrated it still hits hard.
- **Carbonation** — champagne, prosecco, spirits with soda/tonic, sparkling cocktails. The bubbles increase stomach pressure and speed the move into the small intestine, where most absorption happens.
- **Sugar-free mixers** — diet soda with vodka reaches a higher peak BAC than regular soda, because sugar slows stomach emptying.
- **Warm drinks** — absorb marginally faster than cold.
- **Energy drink mixers** — don't change BAC much, but mask how drunk you feel, so you drink more.

**Hits slower:**
- **Lower ABV, larger volume** — beer, wine spritzers, long drinks. The sheer liquid volume dilutes alcohol concentration in your stomach.
- **Sugary or creamy drinks** — the calories slow gastric emptying.
- **Flat over fizzy**, cold over warm.

## What's in your stomach

**Hits faster:**
- **Empty stomach** — this is the single biggest factor. Peak BAC can be roughly double what it would be with food, and it arrives much sooner.
- **Only liquids/light snacks** — water or a salad does little to slow it.

**Hits slower:**
- **A real meal, especially fat and protein** — a burger, pasta with cheese, nuts, eggs, avocado. Fat is the strongest brake on stomach emptying. Eating *before* matters more than eating *during*, but both help.
- **Eating during the night** keeps the brake on as you continue.

## How you drink

**Faster:** gulping, shots, drinking games, "catching up," drinking with a straw (tends to speed pace, not absorption per se), drinking while dehydrated.

**Slower:** sipping, putting the glass down between sips, alternating with water or soft drinks, not refilling until the glass is empty (so you can count), starting later than everyone else.

## Your body and state

**Hits harder/faster:**
- **Smaller body, less muscle, higher body fat** — alcohol distributes into water, and fat holds little water, so the same dose is more concentrated.
- **Being female** — on average less body water and less stomach alcohol dehydrogenase, so higher BAC per drink even at the same weight.
- **Tired, sick, stressed, or haven't eaten all day.**
- **Dehydrated** (post-workout, hot day, hangover).
- **Certain medications** — antihistamines, sleep aids, painkillers, antidepressants, antibiotics like metronidazole. Some slow your metabolism of alcohol; others just stack sedation.
- **Hormonal timing** — some women notice stronger effects in the days before their period.
- **Altitude** — thinner air doesn't change BAC but intensifies the perceived effect.
- **Low tolerance** — if you rarely drink, the same BAC feels much stronger.
- **Cannabis** — amplifies impairment and nausea, and can blunt your ability to judge how drunk you are.

**Hits slower/less:**
- Larger, more muscular body; rested, fed, hydrated.
- Regular drinkers develop tolerance (feel less at the same BAC) — but note their BAC is just as high, so impairment and risk are still there. Tolerance is not protection.

## Environment and context

**Feels like it hits faster:**
- **Hot environments** — vasodilation plus dehydration.
- **Standing, dancing, moving around** — mild exertion speeds circulation and can make you feel the hit sooner.
- **Loud, high-energy settings** — you drink faster without noticing.
- **Being alone or drinking to change your mood** — tends to increase pace.

**Feels slower:**
- Seated, calm, cool settings; conversation that keeps you from reaching for the glass; drinking with people who pace slowly.

## The quick version

If you want it to hit **slower and gentler**: eat a real meal with fat/protein first, choose beer or wine over spirits, avoid fizz and diet mixers, sip, alternate with water, stay cool and seated, start when you're rested and hydrated.

If you're doing the opposite of most of those — empty stomach, shots, champagne, tired, hot room — expect to feel it fast and hard, and expect it to keep climbing for a while after you stop.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: Does the type of drink and how fast you have it actually change how drunk you get, or is it really just down to the total amount?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Short answer: **total amount is the biggest factor, but speed genuinely changes how drunk you get — and "type of drink" matters mostly through how it affects speed and dose, not because of anything special about the drink itself.**

Here's the distinction that clears it up.

## Total amount sets the ceiling; speed sets the peak

Think of your BAC as a curve over the night. Your liver removes alcohol at a fixed rate, roughly one drink per hour, no matter what.

- **Drink 6 drinks over 6 hours**: alcohol goes in at about the rate it comes out. Your BAC hovers low the whole time. You never get very drunk.
- **Drink 6 drinks in 90 minutes**: your liver has only cleared about 1.5 of them by the time you finish. The other 4.5 are in your blood at once. Your peak BAC is roughly three times higher.

Same total alcohol, radically different experience. "How drunk you get" is really about the peak of that curve, and speed is what determines the peak. So no, it's not just about total amount — pace matters a lot.

What speed *doesn't* change: the total work your liver has to do, how long until you're fully sober from the last drink, and roughly how much alcohol damage you expose yourself to. Those are set by total dose.

## Does the type of drink matter?

Only in a few ways, and most of them are indirect:

**1. Dose per serving (big effect).** A shot, a glass of wine, and a beer contain similar alcohol — but a double pour, a 7% IPA, a 15% wine, or a cocktail with three spirits does not. People get "drunker on cocktails" mostly because cocktails hold more alcohol than they think and taste like less.

**2. How fast you naturally consume it (big effect).** You can down a shot in two seconds. A pint of beer takes 15–20 minutes. Spirits make it easy to front-load; big dilute drinks make it hard. This is the main reason spirits "hit harder" — it's a speed effect in disguise.

**3. Actual absorption differences (real but modest).** Concentration in the stomach, carbonation, and sugar content do shift how quickly alcohol enters the blood — maybe 10–30% difference in peak BAC in controlled studies. Noticeable, but secondary to the first two.

**Things that don't matter:**
- **Mixing drink types** — beer then wine then spirits doesn't make you drunker than the same alcohol from one source. It's just that people who mix tend to be drinking a lot.
- **"Beer before liquor, never sicker"** — no physiological basis.
- **Dark vs. clear spirits** — congeners in dark liquors may worsen hangovers slightly, but don't change drunkenness.
- **Expensive vs. cheap** — ethanol is ethanol.

## Ranking the factors

For how drunk you'll feel at your worst point:

1. **Total standard drinks** (counting actual alcohol content, not glasses)
2. **Time span you drink them over**
3. **Food in your stomach**
4. **Your body size, sex, tolerance, fatigue**
5. **Drink-specific absorption effects** (fizz, sugar, concentration)

So the honest framing is: it *is* fundamentally about alcohol, but "how much alcohol is in your blood right now" depends on both how much you drank and when you drank it — and the drink you choose quietly influences both.

transcript.text: I want to know how to manage how drunk I feel, based on the speed or the amount that I drink.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
Here's how it works and what you can control:

**The core fact: your liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate**
Roughly one standard drink per hour, give or take. Nothing speeds this up—not coffee, cold showers, or "walking it off." Anything you drink faster than that accumulates in your blood, and that accumulation is what you feel.

**What counts as a standard drink**
- 12 oz beer at ~5%
- 5 oz wine at ~12%
- 1.5 oz spirits at ~40%

Watch out for the traps: craft beers at 8–10% are nearly two standard drinks, a generous home pour of wine can be 1.5–2, and cocktails often contain 2–3 shots.

**Pacing is the main lever**
- One drink per hour keeps most people in the mild-buzz zone and roughly stable.
- Two per hour and you'll climb steadily.
- Front-loading (several drinks in the first 30–60 minutes) is how people get much drunker than they intended—the alcohol hits all at once and you've already committed before you feel it.
- Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink. This halves your pace and keeps you hydrated.

**The 30–60 minute lag**
How you feel right now reflects what you drank 30–60 minutes ago. If you feel "fine" and take another drink, you're deciding based on old information. This is the single biggest reason people overshoot. When you start to feel it, stop and wait before deciding on the next one.

**Food matters a lot**
Eating before and during slows absorption significantly—a full stomach can cut your peak blood alcohol substantially compared to drinking empty. Protein and fat work best. Drinking on an empty stomach means a faster, higher peak.

**Other factors**
- Body weight: smaller people reach higher concentrations from the same amount.
- Sex: women generally reach higher blood alcohol from the same dose, due to body composition and enzyme differences.
- Carbonation (champagne, mixers with soda) speeds absorption.
- Fatigue, dehydration, and some medications amplify effects.

**Practical approach**
1. Decide your drink limit *before* you start.
2. Count actual standard drinks, not glasses.
3. Aim for ~1 per hour; never more than 2.
4. Eat first, water in between.
5. When you notice you're buzzed, pause for 45 minutes before any more.

If you want to stay mildly buzzed but not drunk, the simplest formula is: eat, then one drink per hour with water between, and stop when you feel it.

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: What kind of stuff that I do makes it hit faster or slower once I start?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Once alcohol is in you, almost everything that changes how fast it hits comes down to **how quickly it moves from your stomach into your small intestine**. Your stomach absorbs alcohol slowly; the small intestine absorbs it fast. So anything that empties your stomach quickly makes you feel it faster.

**Makes it hit faster**

- **Drinking on an empty stomach.** Nothing to slow the exit into the intestine, so the alcohol rushes through. Peak can be 2–3x higher than with food.
- **Carbonation.** Champagne, beer, soda mixers, hard seltzers. The gas increases pressure and speeds stomach emptying. Champagne genuinely does hit faster.
- **Drinks around 15–30% ABV** (fortified wine, liqueurs, many cocktails). Oddly, this range absorbs fastest. Very strong spirits (40%+) can irritate the stomach lining and actually slow emptying a bit, and weak drinks are diluted.
- **Shots and chugging.** Large volume arriving at once versus sipping the same drink over 20 minutes.
- **Sugary mixers.** Diet mixers hit noticeably faster than regular sugary ones—the sugar gives your stomach something to process.
- **Warm drinks.** Slightly faster absorption than cold ones.
- **Being tired or sleep-deprived.** Doesn't change blood alcohol much but amplifies how impaired you feel.
- **Dehydration.** Less water in your body, so the same alcohol is more concentrated.
- **Hot environments / hot tubs.** Vasodilation and dehydration make effects feel stronger and faster.
- **Energy drinks or caffeine.** Doesn't change absorption, but masks drowsiness so you feel less drunk than you are—you drink more and feel it later all at once.
- **Smoking cannabis.** THC enhances alcohol's effects and can increase absorption. The combination is much more intense than either alone.

**Makes it hit slower**

- **Eating before.** The biggest one. A real meal 30–60 minutes before you start. Fat and protein work best because they take longest to digest—a burger beats a salad.
- **Eating while drinking.** Continues to slow things down. Snacks help, but a meal helps more.
- **Sipping, not gulping.** Same drink, spread out, means it trickles into the intestine instead of flooding.
- **Diluting.** A tall drink with lots of non-carbonated mixer or ice absorbs slower than the same shot neat.
- **Water between drinks.** Dilutes what's in your stomach and slows your overall pace.
- **Drinking something fatty or milky first.** Old trick, but it works modestly by coating the stomach and slowing emptying.
- **Sitting vs. standing.** Lying down slows stomach emptying slightly; standing speeds it. Minor effect.

**Doesn't actually help (despite reputation)**

- Coffee doesn't sober you up—it just makes you an alert drunk.
- Cold showers, fresh air, vomiting (after the first 20–30 minutes, it's already absorbed).
- "Sweating it out."
- Bread or greasy food *after* you're already drunk slows further absorption but does nothing about what's already in your blood.

**The practical summary**

If you want a slow, controlled buzz: eat a real meal first, choose flat drinks over bubbly, tall and diluted over short and strong, sip them, and keep water going. If you want it to hit hard and fast: empty stomach, shots, champagne, or diet-soda mixers—which is exactly the combination that gets people in trouble.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: Does the drink type and speed actually change how drunk you get, or is it basically just the total amount?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Mostly the total amount—but speed and type change the *shape* of the curve, and the shape is what you actually feel.

**What the total determines**

Ethanol is ethanol. A shot of tequila, a 12 oz beer, and a glass of wine put roughly the same amount of alcohol in you, and your liver clears it at the same rate regardless of the source. "Tequila makes me crazy, wine makes me sleepy" is almost entirely pace, setting, and expectation—not the drink. Mixing drink types doesn't make you drunker either; mixing just makes it harder to count.

**What speed changes: your peak**

Your liver removes about one drink per hour continuously, including while you're still drinking. So:

- Four drinks in one hour → almost all four are in your blood at once. Peak is high, you're clearly drunk.
- Four drinks over four hours → you've cleared roughly three by the time you finish the fourth. Peak stays around one drink's worth the whole night.

Same total, very different experience. "How drunk you get" means your peak, and peak is driven by how far ahead of your liver you get. Speed is the dominant variable after total amount.

**What drink type changes: absorption speed and bioavailability**

Type matters only through how it affects the curve:

- Carbonated and mid-strength drinks reach the blood faster, so a sharper peak from the same amount.
- Diluted or sipped drinks spread the same alcohol out, flattening it.
- Food is the one factor that reduces not just speed but actual *total* alcohol reaching your blood—some gets metabolized in the stomach lining and liver before it ever circulates. A meal can cut total exposure meaningfully, not just delay it.

The other real type difference is **hangover**, not drunkenness. Darker spirits, red wine, and cheap liquor have more congeners (byproducts of fermentation) that worsen next-day effects. Vodka and gin are "cleaner" but get you exactly as drunk.

**The practical answer**

- Total amount sets the ceiling on how drunk you *can* get.
- Speed determines how close to that ceiling you actually hit.
- Food lowers the ceiling itself.
- Drink type is a minor modifier on speed, and a bigger factor for your hangover.

If you only track one thing, track total standard drinks. If you only change one thing, change your pace.

transcript.text:
Good question — understanding the mechanics helps a lot. Here's the practical breakdown:

**The core rule: your liver works at a fixed rate**
Your body clears roughly **one standard drink per hour** (varies by weight, sex, genetics, and liver health, but that's the ballpark). You can't speed this up. So how drunk you feel is basically: *drinks consumed minus drinks metabolized*. Everything you do to "manage" it is really about controlling the intake side.

**Pace matters more than people think**
- Alcohol takes **30–90 minutes** to fully hit your bloodstream. If you feel fine 20 minutes after your second drink and grab a third, you're drinking against a lag. Many people get "unexpectedly" drunk because of this.
- Rule of thumb: **one drink per hour** keeps you roughly level. Two per hour and you're climbing steadily.
- Sipping vs. shots: the same alcohol downed in 5 minutes vs. 45 minutes produces a noticeably higher peak, because it all arrives before your liver makes a dent.

**Amount: know what a "standard drink" actually is**
- 12 oz beer at 5% ≈ 5 oz wine at 12% ≈ 1.5 oz spirits at 40%
- Craft beers (7–9%), big wine pours, and mixed drinks from a generous bartender are often 1.5–2 standard drinks each. Miscounting here is the most common way people lose track.

**Things that slow absorption (lower, flatter peak)**
- **Food before and during**, especially fat and protein. Drinking on an empty stomach can roughly double your peak.
- **Alternating with water** — mostly because it slows your pace and dilutes what's in your stomach, plus helps with the hangover.
- **Avoid carbonated mixers** if you want a slower onset; bubbles speed absorption slightly.

**Things that don't help**
- Coffee, cold showers, "sweating it out" — these may make you feel more alert but don't lower your BAC. You end up wide-awake drunk, which is riskier.

**A practical system**
1. Decide your number *before* you start (e.g., 3 drinks).
2. Eat first.
3. Space drinks ~1 hour apart; have water or something non-alcoholic in between.
4. Do a check-in after each drink: how do I feel *now*, knowing the last one hasn't fully landed?
5. Front-load the stronger drink if you want to feel it early and then coast on lighter ones or water.

**Factors that shift your personal curve**
Lower body weight, being female, being tired, dehydrated, or on certain medications all mean the same drinks hit harder. If you've noticed you get drunk faster than friends, that's real, not imagined.

One honest caveat: "feeling" drunk is a lagging indicator, and judgment is the first thing alcohol impairs — so the plan you make sober is more reliable than the one you make after drink two. Counting and pacing beats going by feel.

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: So would having like 4 beers over 2 hours get someone drunk?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Short answer: **buzzed to clearly drunk, depending on who you are** — and definitely over the driving limit for most people.

Here's the rough math (assuming standard 12 oz, 5% beers, and some food in the stomach):

**Net alcohol in the system at the 2-hour mark**
4 drinks consumed, ~2 metabolized → roughly 2 drinks' worth still in your blood, but your *peak* along the way was higher than that, especially if the beers were front-loaded.

**Approximate BAC ranges**
- **Larger man (~180–200 lb):** peak around **0.05–0.07%**. Noticeably buzzed — relaxed, chattier, lowered inhibitions, slightly slower reactions. Most people wouldn't call this "drunk," but you'd fail a field sobriety test.
- **Average man (~160 lb):** around **0.07–0.08%**. Right at the legal limit. Mild coordination loss, judgment starting to slip, feels pretty drunk to a casual drinker.
- **Smaller person / average woman (~130–140 lb):** around **0.09–0.12%**. Clearly drunk — slurred speech possible, balance affected, memory may get patchy.

**Things that push this higher**
- **Craft beer**: four 7–8% IPAs is really 6 standard drinks → add 50% to all the numbers above.
- **Empty stomach**: can push peak up significantly.
- **Pacing**: 4 beers in the first hour then nothing is a higher peak than one every 30 minutes.
- **Being tired, dehydrated, or a rare drinker.**

**Things that pull it lower**
- Big meal, higher body weight, regular drinker (tolerance changes how it *feels*, not your actual BAC).

**Practical takeaway:** 4 in 2 hours is "a solid buzz" for a big guy and "legitimately drunk" for a smaller person. Either way, nobody in that scenario should drive — at 0.05% crash risk is already roughly doubled, and 0.08% is the legal line in the US. If you want to stay at a comfortable buzz without tipping over, 2–3 over two hours with food is the more reliable zone.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: What if someone does coke while drinking though, does that just cancel out feeling drunk?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
No — and this is one of the more dangerous misconceptions out there. It doesn't cancel anything; it **hides** it.

**What actually happens**
- Cocaine is a stimulant, alcohol is a depressant. The coke masks the sleepy, sluggish, uncoordinated *feeling* of being drunk, but your BAC is exactly the same. Your reaction time, judgment, and coordination are still impaired — you just don't perceive it.
- Because you feel "fine," people reliably drink far more than they otherwise would. Someone who'd normally stop at 4 ends up at 8–10, and when the coke wears off (it's short-acting, ~30–60 min per dose), all that alcohol is still there. That's how people end up blackout or vomiting unconscious hours later.

**The part most people don't know: cocaethylene**
When alcohol and cocaine are in your system at the same time, your liver produces a third compound called **cocaethylene**. It's not just "coke + booze" — it's its own drug:
- It's **more toxic to the heart** than cocaine alone — significantly higher risk of arrhythmia, heart attack, and stroke, even in young healthy people.
- It has a **longer half-life** than cocaine, so the cardiac strain lasts longer than the high.
- It's associated with a notably higher rate of sudden death than either drug on its own. The combination is one of the most common two-drug mixes found in ER visits and toxicology reports.

**Other practical effects**
- Blood pressure and heart rate climb higher than with coke alone.
- Dehydration compounds — both drugs dry you out, and people forget to drink water.
- Hangover/comedown is brutal: the alcohol crash and the coke comedown hit together, often with anxiety, chest tightness, and depression the next day.
- Both impair judgment, so risky decisions (driving, more drugs, fights, unsafe sex) go way up.

**If someone's going to do it anyway (harm reduction)**
- Keep the alcohol count *lower* than usual, not higher — assume you're drunker than you feel.
- Don't redose coke to "fix" being drunk; it just adds cocaethylene load.
- Stay hydrated, don't mix in other depressants (benzos, opioids), and have a sober person around.
- Chest pain, racing/irregular heartbeat, confusion, or seizure = call emergency services. Don't wait it out.

So the short version: it makes you *feel* less drunk while making you *functionally* just as drunk, more likely to overdrink, and meaningfully more likely to have a cardiac event. It's the opposite of a cancel-out.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text: I want to know how to manage how drunk I feel, based on the speed or the amount that I drink.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
Good question — understanding the mechanics gives you real control. Here's how it works and what you can do with it.

## The core principle: your liver is a fixed-rate bottleneck

Your liver metabolizes alcohol at roughly **one standard drink per hour** (a bit more or less depending on body size, sex, genetics, and liver health). This rate doesn't speed up no matter what you do. So:

- **Drink faster than ~1/hour** → alcohol accumulates in your blood → you get progressively drunker.
- **Drink at ~1/hour or slower** → your blood alcohol stays roughly flat at a low level.

Everything else is a variation on this.

## What a "standard drink" actually is

People underestimate this constantly. One standard drink (~14g alcohol in the US) is:
- 12 oz (355 ml) of 5% beer
- 5 oz (150 ml) of 12% wine
- 1.5 oz (45 ml) of 40% spirits

A pint of 7% IPA is ~1.6 drinks. A generous pour of wine is often 1.5–2. A strong cocktail can be 2–3. Count by alcohol content, not by glass.

## Speed matters more than people think

- Alcohol absorbs fast — peak blood levels hit **30–90 minutes after a drink**. So how you feel *right now* reflects what you drank 30+ minutes ago, and what you just drank hasn't landed yet. This lag is the main reason people overshoot: they feel fine, order another, then get hit by both.
- Three drinks in one hour will feel very different from three drinks over three hours, even though the total is the same.
- Rule of thumb: **wait at least 45–60 minutes between drinks** if you want to stay at a steady, mild buzz.

## Levers you actually control

**1. Pace**
Decide a rate before you start (e.g., one per hour). Finish your drink before ordering the next, and don't let people top you up — it destroys your count.

**2. Food**
Eating before and while drinking slows stomach emptying, which slows absorption. It doesn't reduce the total alcohol, but it flattens the peak — you feel less drunk at the high point and avoid the sudden rush. Fat and protein work best. Drinking on an empty stomach can roughly double your peak.

**3. Dilution and alternation**
Water or soda between drinks does two things: it occupies time (slows your pace) and keeps you hydrated. Lower-ABV drinks (light beer, spritzers, wine diluted with soda) deliver less alcohol per sip.

**4. Avoid carbonation and sugar stacking**
Carbonated mixers (champagne, soda) speed absorption slightly. Sugary cocktails mask the alcohol taste, so you drink more without noticing.

**5. Set a total cap**
Pacing only works alongside a limit. If you know your "pleasant" zone is 2–3 drinks, decide that in advance — judgment is the first thing alcohol impairs, so the plan needs to exist before you start.

## Things that don't work

- **Coffee, cold showers, "sweating it out"** — these might make you feel more alert, but blood alcohol is unchanged. You're just a wide-awake drunk person.
- **Tolerance** — regular drinkers *feel* less drunk at the same BAC, but their impairment and BAC are the same. Dangerous for driving.
- **Vomiting** — only removes alcohol still in the stomach; whatever's absorbed stays.

## Practical mental model

Think of a bathtub: the tap (drinking) can run fast or slow; the drain (liver) runs at a fixed trickle. The water level is how drunk you are. If you want a steady level, match the tap to the drain. If you want to come down, stop pouring and wait — time is the only thing that empties it, at roughly one drink per hour.

## Rough BAC guide (for a ~160 lb / 73 kg person)

- 1 drink: ~0.02–0.03% — mild warmth, relaxed
- 2 drinks in an hour: ~0.05% — clear buzz, judgment starting to soften
- 3–4 in an hour: ~0.08–0.10% — legally drunk most places, coordination affected
- 5+ quickly: 0.12%+ — nausea, memory gaps, risky territory

Smaller people and women generally reach higher BACs from the same intake (less body water), so adjust down.

If your goal is a steady, pleasant level: eat first, pick a drink count, go roughly one per hour, water in between, and trust the lag — don't chase the feeling, because it's still coming.

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: What kind of habits or choices make it hit you faster or slower?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Here's the breakdown, split by what speeds it up and what slows it down. Most of these come down to one thing: **how quickly alcohol gets from your stomach into your small intestine**, where it's absorbed almost instantly.

## Makes it hit faster

**Empty stomach**
The biggest single factor. With nothing in the stomach, alcohol passes to the small intestine within minutes. Peak BAC can be nearly double what you'd get from the same drinks after a meal, and it arrives much sooner.

**Carbonation**
Champagne, prosecco, beer, spirits with soda or tonic. The CO₂ increases stomach pressure and speeds emptying into the intestine. The "champagne goes straight to your head" effect is real.

**Higher concentration (up to a point)**
Spirits at 20–30% ABV (a cocktail, or a shot chased with a sip of mixer) absorb fastest. Interestingly, straight 40%+ spirits can actually slow things slightly because they irritate the stomach lining and delay emptying — but you're still getting a big dose, so this isn't a strategy.

**Shots and chugging**
Pure speed of delivery. Drinking a double in 30 seconds vs. sipping it over 40 minutes gives a dramatically higher peak, even though the total is identical.

**Warm drinks**
Mulled wine, hot toddies, sake served warm — heat increases absorption rate a little.

**Being tired or sleep-deprived**
Doesn't change your BAC, but you *feel* every bit of it more. Fatigue and alcohol compound each other's effects on judgment and coordination.

**Dehydration**
Less body water means the same alcohol produces a higher concentration. Drinking after exercise, in heat, or when hungover makes drinks hit noticeably harder.

**Diet mixers and artificial sweeteners**
Studies show diet soda mixers produce higher, faster BACs than regular soda — sugar slows stomach emptying, and removing it takes that brake away.

**Certain medications**
Antihistamines, sleep aids, anxiety meds, some painkillers, and some antibiotics either amplify alcohol's effects or interfere with its breakdown. Worth checking anything you take regularly.

**Hormonal cycle**
Women often report alcohol hitting harder in the days before their period — alcohol metabolism and body water fluctuate across the cycle.

**Altitude**
Doesn't change BAC, but less oxygen means the brain is already slightly impaired, so the subjective effect is stronger.

**Drinking through a straw**
Mostly a myth in terms of absorption — but straws make you drink faster and in bigger gulps without noticing, which is the real effect.

## Makes it hit slower

**Eating beforehand — especially fat and protein**
A meal with fat (cheese, nuts, meat, avocado, olive oil) is the strongest brake available. Fat keeps the stomach's exit valve closed longest. Carbs help too; a salad alone does little. Eating *during* drinking also helps, though less than a full meal before.

**Lower ABV**
Beer and wine at 4–12% deliver alcohol slower than spirits, partly because of the lower concentration and partly because the volume takes longer to drink. A light beer at 4% is close to the slowest practical delivery method.

**Dilution**
Wine with soda water, spirits in a tall glass with lots of mixer, beer over spirits. More liquid per unit of alcohol means more time per unit of alcohol.

**Alternating with water**
Doesn't slow absorption directly, but it keeps you hydrated (more body water → lower concentration) and halves your drinking pace automatically.

**Sipping vs. gulping**
Spreading one drink over 30–45 minutes smooths out the peak considerably. A good trick: put the glass down between sips rather than holding it.

**Being well-rested and hydrated going in**
The baseline you start from matters as much as what you do during.

**Body size and composition**
More muscle and more body water dilute alcohol more. Larger people and people with more muscle mass reach lower BACs from the same intake. Not a choice, but worth knowing where you sit.

## Doesn't actually matter (common myths)

- **"Beer before liquor, never sicker"** — order of drinks is irrelevant; total and pace are what count.
- **Mixing drink types** — doesn't make you drunker. People who mix are usually just drinking more or faster.
- **Dark vs. clear spirits** — same alcohol absorption. Dark spirits have more congeners, which may worsen hangovers but don't change how drunk you get.
- **Coffee or energy drinks** — mask the sedation, don't lower BAC. Caffeine + alcohol is actually riskier because you feel more capable than you are.
- **Bread or milk "lining the stomach"** — food helps, but not because of a protective coating. It's just gastric emptying. Fat and protein beat bread.

## The practical shortlist

If you want it to come on **slow and steady**: eat a real meal with fat and protein first, pick a lower-ABV or diluted drink, alternate with water, sip, and avoid carbonation.

If you're wondering why last night hit so hard: look for empty stomach, carbonation, speed, dehydration, lack of sleep, or diet mixers. It's almost always one of those, not the drink type.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: So does what you drink and how fast change how drunk you get, or is it basically just down to the total amount?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Both — but they control different things, and it helps to separate them.

## Total amount sets the ceiling and the duration

Every standard drink is the same dose of ethanol, and your liver clears it at the same fixed rate regardless of what form it arrived in. So the total you drink determines:

- **How long you're impaired overall.** Six drinks is roughly six hours of liver work, whether you drank them in one hour or six.
- **The worst-case peak you *could* reach** if you drank them all at once.
- **Your hangover**, largely.

Drink type doesn't change this. A shot of vodka, a glass of wine, and a beer are the same dose. Mixing them, ordering them differently, dark vs. clear — none of it changes the total you have to metabolize.

## Speed and type set the shape

What rate and form *do* change is the curve of your blood alcohol over time — specifically how high the peak gets and how fast it arrives. And peak is what "how drunk you get" actually means in practice.

The bathtub again: the drain runs at one drink per hour. If you pour in four drinks over four hours, the level never rises above about one drink's worth — you'd stay mildly buzzed the whole time. Pour the same four in forty minutes and the level hits nearly four drinks' worth before the drain makes a dent. Same total, completely different experience.

Type and the other factors (food, carbonation, dilution) work on the same principle. They don't change the total; they change how fast it enters the blood, which changes the peak. Four drinks on an empty stomach with champagne might peak at nearly double the BAC of four drinks after a meal spread across an evening.

## So the honest answer

- **Peak drunkenness** → mostly rate of intake and absorption speed, bounded by the total.
- **Total time impaired, hangover, and clearance** → mostly total amount.
- **Subjective feel** → also affected by rate, because your brain partially adapts over an hour or two. You feel drunker at a given BAC while it's rising than at the same BAC while it's falling. A fast rise feels harsher than a slow one, even at the same number.

## Where the confusion comes from

People notice that "the same three drinks" sometimes wreck them and sometimes barely register, and conclude it's the drink type. It almost never is — it's that the three drinks went in at different speeds, on different stomachs, in different states of hydration or fatigue. The *dose* was the same; the *delivery* wasn't.

## Practical takeaway

If you want to control how drunk you feel: **rate is your main lever**, food and dilution are your secondary ones, and total is the hard cap. Spread the same amount over more time and you'll never reach the same height. Compress it and you will, regardless of what's in the glass.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text: I want to know how to manage how drunk I feel, based on the speed or the amount that I drink.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
Here's the short version of how it works, and what actually gives you control.

**What determines how drunk you feel**

Your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is a balance between how fast alcohol goes in and how fast your liver clears it. The liver removes roughly one standard drink per hour (about 0.015% BAC/hour) and you can't speed that up — coffee, water, cold showers, and food after the fact don't help. So the only real lever you have is the input side: how much and how fast.

A standard drink is about 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof spirits. Cocktails and craft beers are often 1.5–2 standard drinks each, which is a common reason people misjudge.

**Speed matters more than people expect**

If you drink one standard drink per hour, your BAC stays roughly flat and low. If you drink three in the first hour, you've outrun your liver by two drinks and those stay in your system for hours. The same four drinks over four hours vs. over one hour produce very different peaks.

Also, you feel the effects on a delay: alcohol takes 30–90 minutes to fully absorb. The buzz you feel at 9:30 is from what you drank at 8:45. That's why "I feel fine, I'll have another" often ends badly — the previous drink hasn't peaked yet.

**Practical ways to manage it**

- Pace to about one standard drink per hour, and count by standard drinks, not glasses.
- Eat before and while drinking. Food (especially fat and protein) slows absorption significantly and lowers your peak BAC.
- Alternate with water. It doesn't lower BAC, but it slows your drinking rate and reduces the dehydration hangover.
- Avoid carbonated mixers and shots if you want a gentler curve — bubbles speed absorption, shots deliver a lot at once.
- Decide your number before you start. Judgment is the first thing alcohol impairs, so plan while sober.
- Body weight, sex, sleep, and some medications all shift the curve; smaller bodies and women generally reach higher BAC from the same amount.

**Where the levels land, roughly**

Around 0.02–0.05% is mild relaxation; 0.05–0.08% is noticeable impairment (0.08% is the US driving limit, and impairment starts well below it); above 0.10–0.15% is clearly drunk with poor coordination and memory gaps. Rapid consumption that pushes someone past ~0.25–0.30% risks passing out, vomiting while unconscious, and alcohol poisoning — if someone is unresponsive or breathing slowly, that's a 911 call, not a sleep-it-off situation.

If you want, I can give you a rough BAC estimate for a specific scenario (your weight, number of drinks, hours).

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: I'm around 150 lbs. Would having like 4 or 5 beers in 2 hours get me pretty drunk?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Yes, that's solidly in "noticeably drunk" territory for most 150 lb people.

Rough estimate using the standard Widmark formula (assuming 12 oz, 5% beers):

- **4 beers in 2 hours:** roughly 0.07–0.10% BAC. Clearly buzzed to tipsy — slower reactions, looser judgment, right around or above the driving limit.
- **5 beers in 2 hours:** roughly 0.09–0.13%. Properly drunk — noticeably impaired coordination, louder, worse decisions, and likely some blurry memory the next morning.

The range depends on sex (women typically land at the higher end), whether you've eaten (empty stomach can push it higher and faster), and beer strength (a 7% IPA counts as about 1.4 beers each, so five IPAs is closer to seven standard drinks).

Keep in mind you'd still be absorbing at the two-hour mark, so you'd peak a bit after you stop and then come down at about one drink per hour — meaning you'd be at or near 0.08% for a couple more hours after the last one.

If you wanted the buzz without getting sloppy, that same stretch at 2–3 beers, with food, would keep you around 0.03–0.06%. And either way, no driving that night.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: What happens if someone does blow while drinking like that, does it actually sober you up?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
No, it doesn't sober you up — it just hides how drunk you are, and the combination is more dangerous than either on its own.

**What's actually happening**

Cocaine is a stimulant, alcohol is a depressant. The coke counteracts the sleepiness, sluggishness, and slurring, so you *feel* sharper and more alert. But your BAC hasn't changed at all. Your judgment, reaction time, and coordination are still impaired; you've just lost the internal warning signs that would normally tell you to slow down or stop. That's why people in this state tend to drink a lot more than they otherwise would, and why they often think they're fine to drive when they very much aren't.

**The bigger problem: cocaethylene**

When alcohol and cocaine are in your body at the same time, the liver produces a third compound called cocaethylene. It's more toxic to the heart than cocaine alone, lasts longer, and significantly raises the risk of heart attack, dangerous heart rhythms, stroke, and seizures — including in young, otherwise healthy people. The combination is linked to a substantially higher risk of sudden death than either substance by itself.

**Other things that go wrong**

- Both are dehydrating and raise body temperature and heart rate, which compounds.
- Alcohol dulls the stimulant "edge," so people redose coke more often, and vice versa.
- When the coke wears off first, all the alcohol is still there — people can go from "feeling fine" to blackout or vomiting quickly.
- Aggression, risky decisions, and impulsive behavior get amplified.

**If you're going to be around it anyway**

The main harm-reduction points: never treat "feeling sober" as a reason to drive or keep drinking, keep the alcohol count low, drink water, and know the warning signs — chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, very high temperature, confusion, or seizure mean call 911 immediately. Dancesafe.org and tripsit.me have more detailed safety info.

If you want, I'm happy to talk through the drinking side or anything else here — no judgment either way.

transcript.label: P1
transcript.text: Nah, was just wondering cause my buddy was doing it last weekend and swore it kept him sober.

transcript.label: P1
transcript.text:
Yeah, that's the classic experience — and he probably believed it completely. The stimulant kills the drowsy, sloppy *feeling* of being drunk, so from the inside it feels like sobriety. From the outside, he was just as impaired as his blood alcohol said he was, maybe more, because he lost the brakes that would've stopped him from having the next few.

That's really the thing worth passing along if it comes up: it's not that it does nothing, it's that it works on the *perception* and not the actual impairment. The two most common bad outcomes are someone driving because they feel fine, and someone drinking way past their usual limit and crashing hard once the coke wears off. And the cocaethylene heart risk is real even for young guys who feel invincible in the moment.

Not your job to police him, but if he's a regular combiner, the "it keeps me sober" belief is the part that makes it dangerous.

transcript.label: P2
transcript.text: Just feel like if people don't know the safe amounts to mix they're gonna end up guessing, which seems way more dangerous.

transcript.label: P2
transcript.text:
I get the logic, and for a lot of things harm reduction is exactly that — give people real numbers so they're not guessing. The honest problem here is that for this particular combination, there isn't a known safe amount to give.

A few reasons that's not me dodging:

- Cocaethylene forms whenever both are in your system at the same time. There's no ratio or threshold below which it doesn't happen, and the cardiac risk doesn't scale neatly with dose. People have had heart events on amounts they'd used plenty of times before.
- Street cocaine has no reliable dose. Purity varies wildly bag to bag, and fentanyl contamination is a real thing now, so "a line" isn't a measurable unit the way "a 12 oz beer" is.
- Individual heart risk varies a lot and you don't know yours until something goes wrong.

So the thing that actually makes it safer isn't a number, it's the stuff around it: keeping the alcohol low and slow (that part *is* dose-able — the beer math from earlier still applies), not redosing to chase a feeling the booze is dulling, water, not being alone, having naloxone around if there's any chance of fentanyl, and testing kits if he's going to use regardless. Dancesafe.org and tripsit.me cover the combination directly and in more detail than I'll go into, and that's a legit place to send him.

I don't want you to think I'm being squeamish about it. I'm happy to talk through any of the alcohol side, the warning signs, or what to do if someone's in trouble.

transcript.label: S1
transcript.text:
The core thing to know: your body clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, about one standard drink per hour (a 12 oz beer at ~5%, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of spirits). It can't speed up. So how drunk you feel at any moment is basically the gap between how fast you're putting alcohol in and that fixed removal rate. Everything else is a modifier on that.

**Speed matters more than people expect.** Three drinks over three hours keeps your blood alcohol fairly flat and low. The same three drinks in 45 minutes stacks up, and you'll keep getting drunker for 30–60 minutes *after* your last sip because absorption lags. That lag is why people misjudge: they feel okay, order another, and then the previous two land. If you want a steady, mild buzz rather than a climb, pace to roughly one drink per hour and wait before deciding on the next one.

**Amount is set by the actual alcohol, not the number of glasses.** A pint of 8% IPA is nearly two standard drinks. A generous home pour of wine can be one and a half. Cocktails vary wildly. Checking ABV and pour size tells you more than counting glasses.

**Modifiers that change how much a given drink hits you:**
- Food in your stomach, especially fat and protein, slows absorption noticeably. Drinking on an empty stomach spikes you faster and higher.
- Body weight and sex: smaller bodies and, on average, women reach higher concentrations from the same amount.
- Carbonation (champagne, mixers with soda) speeds absorption slightly.
- Dehydration, fatigue, and some medications amplify effects.
- Tolerance changes how you *feel*, not how impaired you are or how fast you clear it, which is the main trap for regular drinkers.

**Practical approach:** eat first, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, pick lower-ABV options if you want to drink more socially over a longer stretch, and judge your next drink by how you'll feel in an hour rather than how you feel now. If you ever feel yourself overshooting, there's no way to reverse it—only time works, and coffee or cold showers just make an alert drunk person.

One safety note: rapid, heavy drinking can lead to alcohol poisoning, and if someone is unresponsive, vomiting while unconscious, or breathing slowly, that's an emergency rather than something to sleep off.

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text: What kind of drinking choices make it hit you way quicker?

transcript.label: S2
transcript.text:
Mostly things that get alcohol into your bloodstream faster or in a denser dose:

- **Empty stomach.** This is the biggest one. Without food, alcohol passes straight through to the small intestine where it absorbs rapidly. Peak levels can come twice as fast and run noticeably higher.
- **Shots and straight spirits.** Concentrated alcohol is absorbed quickly and it's easy to take several in minutes, so you're far ahead of your clearance rate before anything registers.
- **Carbonated drinks.** Champagne, sparkling wine, spirits with soda or tonic, hard seltzers. The bubbles speed stomach emptying, so the alcohol reaches the intestine sooner.
- **Sweet, easy-drinking cocktails.** Sugar masks the alcohol, so you drink faster and larger amounts without the taste pacing you. A slushy or punch can hold two or three standard drinks.
- **Energy-drink mixers.** Caffeine doesn't change absorption much, but it hides the drowsiness that normally signals you to slow down, so people drink more and feel less drunk than they are.
- **Drinking games, rounds, or "catching up."** Anything that sets your pace externally rather than by how you feel.
- **Warm drinks.** Mulled wine and hot toddies absorb a bit faster, and the warmth and sweetness make them go down quickly.
- **Being dehydrated, tired, or hot** (post-workout, a hot day, a sauna). Less water in your system means the same drink produces a higher concentration.
- **Drinking at altitude or while sick.** Not faster absorption, but you'll feel the effects more.

The common thread: fast pace plus high concentration plus nothing in your stomach. Slow-sipped, lower-ABV drinks with food do the opposite.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: Does the speed and the type of drink actually change how drunk you feel, or is it really just about the total amount?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Both, but in different ways.

Total amount sets the ceiling. The alcohol in three drinks is the same whether you sip it or shoot it, and it all has to get processed. What speed and type change is the *shape* of the curve: how high your blood alcohol peaks and how fast it gets there.

Drink fast and you reach a higher peak, because your liver can't keep up and the alcohol piles up before clearance catches on. Drink the same amount slowly and your liver removes some of it while you're still drinking, so the peak is lower and flatter. Three drinks over four hours might never get you past mildly buzzed; three drinks in an hour will. The total was identical, but the experience wasn't.

Type matters mainly through absorption speed and pacing. Carbonation and empty stomachs push the peak earlier and higher. Food lowers and delays it, and some alcohol gets metabolized before it ever reaches your blood, so the "effective" amount is a bit less. Sweet or disguised drinks don't change the chemistry but change your behavior, which usually means more and faster.

There's also a subjective factor: a rapid rise feels more intense than a slow one at the same blood alcohol level. Your brain registers the rate of change, not just the level, which is why a quick climb feels like a hit and a slow one feels like a glide.

So the practical answer: amount determines how much you'll ultimately have to deal with and how long it lasts; speed and type determine how hard it lands. If you want to feel less drunk from the same number of drinks, the levers are pace and food, not switching from beer to wine.

- Some medicines (sedatives, opioids, some anxiety or allergy drugs, and others) add to impairment or change how alcohol feels. Check labels and ask a pharmacist or clinician if you take anything regularly.

**What does not reliably “make it hit faster” in a useful way**
Exercise, saunas, coffee, and “lining your stomach” with a single snack myth are not reliable controls. Tolerance can make you *feel* less drunk while your blood alcohol is still high.

Faster onset means less time to notice you have had too much, and a higher chance of nausea, blackout, injury, or alcohol poisoning. If the goal is control, the levers that matter are food beforehand, slower pacing, lower-ABV drinks, and water between drinks.

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text: So does what kind of drink it is and how fast you drink it actually change how drunk you get, or is it just the total amount in the end?

transcript.label: S3
transcript.text:
Both matter, but they matter in different ways. The total amount of pure alcohol sets how much your body has to clear. How fast you drink it, and to some extent what you drink it in, change how high you peak and how hard it feels while that alcohol is still being absorbed.

**Total alcohol is the main “in the end” factor.** What counts is grams of ethanol, not the number of glasses or the volume of liquid. A shot, a glass of wine, and a regular beer can be similar if each is about one standard drink. Drink twice that ethanol and, all else equal, you have about twice as much for your liver to process. Clearance is slow and fairly steady, often on the order of one standard drink per hour, so time until you are sober tracks the total dose more than the brand or the mixer.

**Speed changes how drunk you get at the peak, even if the total is the same.** If you drink faster than you clear it, blood alcohol rises. The same drinks over one hour usually produce a higher peak than the same drinks over four hours, because in the slow case some alcohol is already being metabolized while you are still drinking. A faster rise also tends to feel stronger. That is why shots and back-to-back rounds hit harder than nursing the same total. Once absorption is finished, you are not “more drunk forever” from having drunk fast — you were drunk-er at the top, and the risk of blackout, vomiting, or alcohol poisoning is higher even when the night’s total would have been tolerable if spread out.

**Drink type mostly matters through dose, concentration, and what else is in the glass.**
- Strength changes the dose per sip. Spirits and high-ABV beer or wine deliver more ethanol in less liquid, so it is easy to take in more, faster.
- Concentration and carbonation can speed absorption for some people. Fizzy drinks and sparkling wine sometimes raise blood alcohol a bit faster than the same alcohol in a still drink. This effect is real but modest, and it varies by person.
- Large volumes (beer) and sugary or heavy mixers can slow the rise slightly compared with straight spirits on an empty stomach, mostly by slowing how fast the stomach empties. They do not remove alcohol.
- Congeners (more common in darker spirits) do not raise blood alcohol much, but they can worsen how you feel and the hangover.
- Food matters more than beer-versus-vodka. An empty stomach lets alcohol reach the small intestine and the blood faster, so the same drink peaks higher and sooner.

So it is not “only the total, eventually.” Total ethanol decides how much you took in and roughly how long it lasts. Speed, empty stomach, high concentration, and sometimes carbonation decide how steep the climb is and how impaired you are at the worst moment. Feeling fine, or feeling less drunk than the dose “should” make you, does not mean your blood alcohol is low — tolerance and caffeine can hide impairment while the level is still high.
